newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Solidarity bares teeth in nationwide protest.
newsitem.headline: Polish Solidarity bares teeth in nationwide protest.

text.p: Poland's Solidarity launched nationwide protests to defend the bankrupt Gdansk shipyard on Wednesday and union chiefs threatened a sharp response when riot police acted to oust workers occupying Warsaw ministries.

While about 2,000 demonstrating shipyard workers in Gdansk furiously bricked up the door to an office of the ruling ex-communist party, which Solidarity blames for allowing the yard's collapse, dozens of workers in Warsaw moved in to the Economy, Treasury and Labour ministries early in the day.

Union regional chiefs meeting in Warsaw agreed on plans to escalate the campaign of protests and pickets, launched on Wednesday after a receiver this month announced plans to wind up the shipyard where Solidarity arose in 1980 and based its campaign leading to the 1989 fall of communism.

Just as union leader Marian Krzaklewski and others were about to start a news conference in Warsaw, Solidarity members reported that riot police had entered the occupied ministry buildings and given the workers a 20-minute ultimatum to quit.

"Once more the Red authorities are using force against a peaceful demonstration," leader Kazimierz Grajcarek told the conference, adding that union reinforcements were converging on the capital from elsewhere.

"What is happening in Warsaw is clearly a provocation," said Krzaklewski, head of the union and of the rightist Solidarity Election Action (AWS) it has formed to try to beat the ex-communists in parliamentary polls later this year.
PAP news agency later reported that the workers had left or been removed from all three buildings by police and that some had been slightly injured at the Treasury.

Krzaklewski said the union regional chiefs were reconvening their meeting to decide their response to the incidents and added that the union could call a general strike if force was used against it, although it would try other options first.
Solidarity's protest campaign aims to force a rescue of the shipyard and help for other workers facing job losses in industries such as coal mining in the southern Silesia region.

It is also helping to stir up emotions in the run-up to the election by recalling the pre-1989 communist antecedents of the dominant Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) which has shared power in coalition with a Peasant party since 1993.
Gdansk workers have been demonstrating since the bankrupt yard's receiver announced earlier this month he would dismiss its last 3,800 employees and sell the assets piecemeal.
The receiver acted after banks refused $100 million in credit to finance construction of five ships for a German shipowner, which could have kept the Baltic coast yard going.

The government did not encourage these credits, arguing that the ship contracts were deeply unsatisfactory, and Solidarity accuses it of failing to act in order to destroy the cradle of Solidarity which is now an opposition stronghold.
But Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz on Tuesday met chiefs of Poland's merchant navy firm PZM and the successful Szczecin shipyard to find ways to save some of the Gdansk jobs.

His spokeswoman declined to reveal the outcome and said Cimoszewicz would inform parliament on Thursday, but Gdansk radio reported that the Szczecin yard may build ships in Gdansk for the Polska Zegluga Morska (PZM) company.
